mechanism.mechanismSummary: Liraglutide is a synthetic glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist analog used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, prevention of cardiovascular complications associated with diabetes, and obesity.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Liraglutide is a synthetic glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist analog used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus, prevention of cardiovascular complications associated with diabetes, and obesity.

The FDA-approved Victoza (liraglutide) label states it is indicated (1) as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and (2) to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease.

The FDA-approved Saxenda (liraglutide 3 mg/day) label states it is indicated, in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, to reduce excess body weight in (a) adults and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with body weight above 60 kg and obesity, and (b) adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbid condition.

Both Victoza and Saxenda (liraglutide) carry an FDA boxed warning that liraglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents at clinically relevant exposures, with human relevance undetermined; liraglutide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2), and in patients with serious hypersensitivity to liraglutide or its excipients.

The Victoza label documents reports of acute pancreatitis (including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis), gastrointestinal adverse reactions (sometimes severe), acute gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis/cholecystitis), increased hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue, and rare reports of pulmonary aspiration during elective surgery in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists.

In the LEADER trial (liraglutide vs. placebo added to standard care in 9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk), the primary composite cardiovascular outcome (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke) occurred in fewer patients in the liraglutide group (608 of 4,668 patients, 13.0%) than in the placebo group (694 of 4,672 patients, 14.9%), hazard ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.97, p=0.01 for superiority); this trial underlies Victoza's cardiovascular risk-reduction indication.

A CADTH clinical review of Saxenda's pivotal SCALE phase 3 trials found statistically significant placebo-adjusted body-weight reductions with liraglutide 3 mg, including a treatment difference of −5.39% (95% CI −5.82 to −4.95, p<0.0001) in the main trial (Study 1839), with odds of achieving ≥5% weight loss about 4.8-fold higher than placebo (OR 4.80, 95% CI 4.12–5.60, p<0.0001). The same review flagged evidence gaps: underrepresentation of patients with BMI 27 to <30 kg/m2, a lack of comparative (head-to-head) evidence, and trial populations that were predominantly White and female, limiting generalizability.

Illegal online sellers market GLP-1 agonist injectables — the drug class that includes liraglutide — without requiring a valid prescription, and some sellers evade enforcement by labeling products 'peptides' intended 'for research purposes only' and 'not for human consumption.' Substandard and falsified GLP-1 products have been identified in multiple countries. Separately, FDA states that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and have not undergone FDA review for safety, effectiveness, or quality. No human outcome data support unsupervised, non-prescription self-administration of liraglutide-class products obtained through these channels, and such use falls outside any FDA-approved label.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: TRULICITY (dulaglutide) is FDA-approved as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years of age and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and separately to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who have established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors. The current label contains no approved indication for weight loss or obesity.

TRULICITY carries a boxed warning that dulaglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors in rats and that it is unknown whether it causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans. It is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2), and in patients with prior serious hypersensitivity to dulaglutide or any product component.

The TRULICITY label warns that acute pancreatitis, including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis, has been observed in patients treated with GLP-1 receptor agonists including dulaglutide, and that postmarketing reports of acute kidney injury (in some cases requiring hemodialysis) have occurred, most often in patients experiencing GI adverse reactions leading to dehydration. Common adverse reactions occurring at >=5% incidence include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and decreased appetite.

Dulaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist consisting of a GLP-1 analog fused to a modified human IgG4 Fc fragment, engineered to slow renal clearance and support once-weekly subcutaneous dosing; DrugBank lists its clinical indication as management of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Per FDA-approved labeling (trial-protocol/label context, not a use recommendation), the recommended starting dosage of TRULICITY for glycemic control is 0.75 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly; after at least 4 weeks, dosage may be increased to 1.5 mg weekly, with further 1.5 mg increments possible at intervals of at least 4 weeks up to a maximum of 4.5 mg once weekly.

In the REWIND randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcomes trial in adults with type 2 diabetes aged >=50 years (with or without established cardiovascular disease), dulaglutide treatment was associated with a significantly lower risk of the primary composite endpoint (non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or cardiovascular death) versus placebo over a median follow-up of 5.4 years (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.79-0.99).

Dulaglutide (Trulicity) has no FDA-approved indication for weight loss or obesity management, unlike some other GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide/Wegovy, tirzepatide/Zepbound) that hold dedicated weight-management approvals; consumer health coverage confirms it is sometimes prescribed off-label for weight loss based on the weight-reduction side effect observed in diabetes trials, but this use sits outside its approved indication and outside the controlled evidence base reviewed here for that specific purpose.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Exenatide is FDA-approved, as the immediate-release twice-daily product (Byetta) and the extended-release once-weekly product (Bydureon / Bydureon BCise), as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults (and, for Bydureon, pediatric patients aged 10 years and older) with type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is not approved as a weight-loss product and concurrent use of multiple exenatide-containing products is not recommended. Note: the manufacturer (AstraZeneca) discontinued Byetta and Bydureon BCise for commercial reasons in October 2024; the underlying FDA approval and labeling remain on file, but as of this writing these exact branded products are no longer commercially marketed in the US.

Both Bydureon and Bydureon BCise carry a boxed warning that exenatide extended-release caused an increased incidence of thyroid C-cell tumors in rats at clinically relevant exposures; human relevance is unknown, and the products are contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

Exenatide is a 39-amino-acid peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist derived from exendin-4 (originally isolated from Gila monster saliva); it binds and activates the human GLP-1 receptor to enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

Per FDA-approved labeling, Byetta's studied and approved dosing regimen is 5 mcg administered subcutaneously twice daily within 60 minutes before the two main meals of the day (approximately 6 or more hours apart), with an increase to 10 mcg twice daily after one month based on clinical response. This is label/trial dosing context, not a use recommendation.

In EXSCEL, a large randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled cardiovascular outcomes trial in adults with type 2 diabetes (n=14,752, broad cardiovascular risk range), once-weekly exenatide met the prespecified noninferiority margin for the primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, or nonfatal stroke) versus placebo (hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.83-1.00) but did not achieve statistical superiority over placebo for that outcome.

In the EXSCEL trial, once-weekly exenatide showed no significant difference from placebo in rates of acute pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, or medullary thyroid carcinoma, and no adverse heart-failure signal despite a higher mean heart rate in the exenatide group.

Exenatide is approved only for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes; unlike newer GLP-1 products approved for weight management, exenatide does not carry an FDA-approved weight-loss indication. Popular online narratives that group exenatide with weight-loss-focused GLP-1 peptides risk projecting a benefit onto it that its own labeling and the identified controlled trial evidence do not establish for that use.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA-approved sermorelin acetate injection (brand GEREF) was indicated for treatment of idiopathic growth hormone deficiency in children with growth failure; the manufacturer (EMD Serono) discontinued the product in 2008, and FDA formally determined the product was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.

As of the access date, no sermorelin or sermorelin acetate drug product is listed in DailyMed (the NLM/FDA labeling repository), and sermorelin/sermorelin acetate does not appear in FDA's Category 2 table of bulk drug substances presenting significant safety risks or in the table of substances nominated but withdrawn on the FDA 503A bulk substances page; there is currently no FDA-approved sermorelin product on the market.

Sermorelin (acetate) is a synthetic 29-amino-acid peptide corresponding to the amino-terminal, biologically active segment of native human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH); it acts as a GHRH-receptor agonist on the anterior pituitary to stimulate endogenous growth hormone secretion.

The only FDA-approved sermorelin products were GEREF injection formulations (0.5 mg base/vial and 1.0 mg base/vial for pediatric GHD treatment; 0.05 mg base/amp for diagnostic testing of pituitary somatotroph GH secretory capacity); both were discontinued by the manufacturer in the 2000s and are no longer manufactured, so sermorelin currently reaches consumers only as a compounded or research-labeled product outside the FDA-approved supply chain.

Controlled human trial evidence specific to sermorelin/GHRH(1-29) in adults is limited: a small 1997 trial (11 healthy men, 64-76 years, 6 weeks of single nightly GHRH(1-29) injections) found improvement in only 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure, with no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, weight, BMI, or waist-to-hip ratio; a separate 2006 trial (89 healthy older adults, 6 months of daily GHRH treatment) found improved cognition on some measures (novel problem-solving, psychomotor/processing speed, working memory) but no improvement on 3 of 6 cognitive tests and no effect on sleep. Neither trial supports general anti-aging, well-being, insulin-sensitivity, or libido claims, and both are old, small, and use GHRH(1-29)/sermorelin rather than the compounded products currently marketed. Consumer-health reporting on sermorelin itself states that adult studies are limited and that definitive research supporting anti-aging benefits is lacking.

Sermorelin is popularly marketed online as a 'pro-aging support therapy' that 'restores your body's natural hGH production' and may increase general well-being, lean body mass, insulin sensitivity, and libido. The libido, insulin-sensitivity, general-well-being, and 'restores natural hGH production'/anti-aging framing are not supported by any controlled human trial identified for sermorelin/GHRH(1-29). The lean-body-mass claim specifically is also not supported: the one located controlled trial that measured body composition (Vittone et al. 1997, 11 elderly men) found no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, though it did find improvement on 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure. A separate controlled trial (Vitiello et al. 2006, 89 older adults) found improved cognition on some measures, which is not among the marketing claims evaluated here. None of this rises to evidence for the marketing claims as stated, and sermorelin's sole historical FDA-approved indication was pediatric growth hormone deficiency, now discontinued; these marketing claims should not be read as proven benefits.

primaryMechanisms: MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded within mitochondrial DNA (within the 12S rRNA region) that acts via AMPK-dependent signaling; in mice it regulates skeletal-muscle metabolism and nuclear genes related to metabolism and proteostasis, and endogenous MOTS-c is exercise-inducible, rising in circulation during and after acute exercise in humans.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: MOTS-c was nominated for FDA's 503A Bulk Drug Substances list but the nomination was withdrawn; FDA's own note on the withdrawn-nominations table states it identified no human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration and lacks information on whether MOTS-c would cause harm if administered to humans, while also flagging potential immunogenicity risk from peptide-related impurities.

In its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) briefing document evaluating MOTS-c (free base) and MOTS-c acetate for the 503A Bulks List, FDA staff state they did not identify any clinical studies or human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration, and that both forms are not well-characterized from a physical/chemical characterization standpoint due to unavailable data on impurities, aggregates, and endotoxins; FDA staff recommended against adding either form to the list. At the PCAC meeting on July 23, 2026, the committee voted 7-5 with 2 abstentions to recommend MOTS-c for the 503A Bulks List, overriding the staff recommendation. An advisory committee vote is not itself a legal listing decision -- FDA must still complete rulemaking before MOTS-c could be lawfully compounded under 503A -- and the staff's underlying findings on the absence of human exposure data and incomplete characterization remain unchanged by the vote.

MOTS-c is a 16-amino-acid peptide encoded within mitochondrial DNA (within the 12S rRNA region) that acts via AMPK-dependent signaling; in mice it regulates skeletal-muscle metabolism and nuclear genes related to metabolism and proteostasis, and endogenous MOTS-c is exercise-inducible, rising in circulation during and after acute exercise in humans.

No published controlled human study of exogenously administered MOTS-c establishing efficacy for metabolic, fat-loss, exercise-performance, or anti-aging outcomes was identified; the only human MOTS-c data located is observational measurement of endogenous (naturally produced) circulating MOTS-c rising during exercise, and FDA's own review found no clinical studies or human exposure data for administered MOTS-c. The physical-capacity and healthspan benefits reported for MOTS-c are from mouse studies only.

An investigational Phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT07505745) is recruiting adults aged 18-65 with BMI 27-40 kg/m2 and documented prediabetes to receive investigational MOTS-c or matching placebo via subcutaneous injection once daily for 12 weeks alongside standardized lifestyle counseling, to evaluate improvement in insulin sensitivity; results are not yet available.

Gray-market peptide vendor content promotes self-administered MOTS-c dosing protocols (e.g., titrating from roughly 2.5-5 mg subcutaneously several times weekly up to a 10 mg five-times-weekly maintenance regimen, timed 30-60 minutes before exercise) and attributes fat-loss, exercise-mimetic, and anti-aging benefits to it, while citing mouse data and a single small uncontrolled/early-phase human observation as support; this marketing framing outruns the human evidence base, which FDA and the primary literature reviewed here describe as absent for administered MOTS-c.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin, brand name Zadaxin) has no FDA-approved drug label in the United States - DailyMed, the authoritative U.S. label repository, returns zero results for "thymalfasin" - and is available in the U.S. only through compounding, not as an approved product; it is approved as a marketed drug in dozens of other countries (commonly cited for hepatitis B/C and as a cancer/vaccine adjuvant), but that ex-U.S. approval status has not been independently verified here against a primary foreign regulator source.

FDA's evaluation of thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1, free base and acetate) for the 503A compounding Bulks List found that a balancing of the four evaluation criteria weighs against adding it, citing insufficient physicochemical characterization, an immunogenicity risk potentially amplified by aggregation and peptide-related impurities, and a proposed injectable concentration (3 mg/mL) that exceeds Ta1 free base's aqueous solubility (2 mg/mL); the nomination was subsequently withdrawn and FDA is evaluating the substance at its own discretion rather than under a completed rulemaking.

FDA's bulk drug substance evaluation flags a potential safety concern specific to immunosuppressed patients: thymosin alpha-1's immune-stimulating activity could cause or worsen acute or chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and lead to engraftment failure in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients.

Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) is a synthetically manufactured 28-amino-acid acetylated polypeptide identical to a naturally occurring human thymic peptide; it is described as activating toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling on dendritic cells, driving Th1 polarization and T-cell maturation as part of coordinated adaptive immune responses.

In the largest and most rigorous published human efficacy trial - TESTS, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults with sepsis across 22 Chinese centers - subcutaneous thymosin alpha-1 every 12 hours for up to 7 days did not reduce 28-day all-cause mortality versus placebo (23.4% vs 24.1%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77-1.27, p=0.93), and secondary/safety outcomes showed no significant differences between groups.

An earlier, smaller multicenter randomized controlled trial (ETASS, six Chinese hospitals, n=361 ICU patients with severe sepsis, 2008-2010) reported a numerically lower 28-day death rate with thymosin alpha-1 added to conventional therapy versus conventional therapy alone (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54-1.02), a difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance, alongside greater improvement in monocyte HLA-DR expression (an immune-function marker) in the treatment group.

Thymosin alpha-1 is marketed and discussed online as having been "long recognized for modifying, enhancing, and restoring immune function," with popular interest extending to autoimmune disease management, general inflammation reduction, cancer support, and longevity-adjacent uses such as long COVID; the only large, rigorous, placebo-controlled human trial identified for a systemic-immunomodulation indication (sepsis) found no mortality benefit, and consumer-facing sources themselves acknowledge that findings for these broader immune/longevity uses are based on small trials and that "more research is needed." No controlled human evidence for general immune optimization, anti-aging, or wellness use in healthy adults was identified in this review.
